catalog_quote: [Patin 2016:290] To conclude this section, I will briefly discuss stress in Shingazidja, since stress will be of notable importance for some aspects of this study (see Section 3.3.1). As in several closely related languages such as Swahili (Ashton (1944), among many others), stress falls regularly on the penult of words. However, stress also relates to the Phonological Phrase in the sense that it seems to be strengthened on the penult of prosodic phrases: in (7a), for instance, the penult of tʃaí ‘tea’ is longer and more intense than the penultimate syllable of the preceding verb. To my knowledge, only one phonetic study has been conducted on stress in Shingazidja: Rey (1990). ... Thus, a detailed study of stress in Shingazidja still remains to be done. Such a study would have to determine the precise nature of the interactions between stress and tones. Indeed, numerous examples in my c…
sweep_summary: Four works with stress in the title, all about the Shingazidja pitch accent ('accent' = H-tone/metrical) system rather than plain word stress. New open download: Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1989 (SLS 19, whole-volume PDF from IDEALS, text) — read in full; it analyses the nominal H-tone system with feet, Meeussen's Rule, final-syllable extrametricality and default H on the penult of toneless words; no separate stress statement; refines (does not contradict) the catalog's penult coding. Rey 1990 thesis: theses.fr record only (not accessible online), abstract read — the only experimental study (duration/F0/intensity) of Shingazidja accent, words 'oxyton ou paroxyton'; high acquisition priority. Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 (CLS 28) and Philippson 2005 (RMCA volume): no open copy anywhere checked (Crossref, Semantic Scholar, HAL, IDEALS, RMCA); print only, medium priority. Also read from the sibling mwal1237 folder: Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1997 ROA-176 (Swahili replaced tone with penultimate stress, Shingazidja retained tonal contrasts) and Philippson 1991 thesis (Comorian 'purement accentuelle', obligatory penult feet even without a marked syllable; Ngazidja feet grouped by two). Nothing read supersedes Patin 2016 as the deciding stress source; the caution that the 'accent' literature is about the pitch system stands.

new_statements.reading: First-hand elicited study, but of the pitch accent (H-tone + metrical foot) system, not of stress: final syllables are extrametrical unless H-toned, and toneless words get their inserted prominence on the penult. It does not describe an independent word stress (the authors explicitly defer phonetic implementation, note 1 p.60). It is consistent with the catalog's penult coding as a default prominence, but the catalog's deciding source (Patin 2016 p.290: stress regularly on the penult, strengthened at the phrase penult, alongside the H-tone system) remains the only explicit stress statement read for this language.

new_statements.quote: Dans les limites de ce travail, il apparait que la place de l'accent est predictible selon des regles phonologiques. L'analyse structuraliste genere la place de l'accent dans le mot, l'analyse metrique propose une hierarchie des accents dans la phrase. [...] Cette relation est fonction principalement de deux variables (toutes choses etant egales par ailleurs): la structure syntaxique de l'enonce (phenomene de joncture),la place de l'accent dans le mot (mot oxyton ou paroxyton). Enfin, ces resultats experimentaux tendent a confirmer les hypotheses au sujet de l'evolution de cette langue, anciennement tonale, devenue a accent.
new_statements.translation: Within the limits of this work, it appears that the position of the accent is predictable by phonological rules. The structuralist analysis generates the position of the accent in the word; the metrical analysis proposes a hierarchy of accents in the sentence. [...] This relation depends mainly on two variables (all else being equal): the syntactic structure of the utterance (juncture phenomenon) and the position of the accent in the word (oxytone or paroxytone word). Finally, these experimental results tend to confirm the hypotheses about the evolution of this language, formerly tonal, which has become accentual.

Reading: the abstract states placement is predictable by phonological rule and that words are 'oxyton ou paroxyton', but names no default and no rule, so unclear or contr…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penult coding as the paroxytone class, but the abstract explicitly recognises an oxytone (final-accented) word class, i.e. accent is final or penult by phonological rule rather than uniformly penult; this matches Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1989 (final syllables extrametrical unless H-toned; H-final words are final-prominent) and Patin 2018's tone-vs-stress account. Full text (which states the actual rules and the instrumental results) is not accessible online.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the abstract: the whole thesis is about accent in Shingazidja; accent placement is predictable by phonological rules; words are either oxytone (final accent) or paroxytone (penult accent); the experimental part (duration, F0, intensity, one speaker, declaratives) treats accent as a tonic/post-tonic relation between syllables, modulated by syntactic juncture; the language is analysed as formerly tonal, now accentual. The abstract does not state which of final/penult is the default or what rule selects them, so the reading cannot be pinned from the abstract alone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Abstract mentions 'une hierarchie des accents dans la phrase' (metrical hierarchy of accents at sentence level), no word-level secondary stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Two word classes: 'mot oxyton ou paroxyton' (final-accented vs penult-accented words).
new_statements.identity_note: Both theses describe Shingazidja of Grande Comore (Ngazidja); Rey 1990 says 'parler de la Grande Comore' and its instrumental data come from one speaker (per Patin 2021 note 3); Patin's 2018 paper held by the project specifies Washili Shingazidja, but his 2007 thesis abstract names no dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Patin, Cédric (2016). La liaison tonale en shingazidja septentrional. Linguistique et Langues Africaines 2: 95-114. Paris: LLACAN (online: OpenEdition Journals). DOI 10.4000/lla.12000.
tone_statements.quote: Le système tonal du shingazidja est bien connu ; ... Cette langue présente un système dit ‘privatif’ (cf. Hyman 2001), dans lequel un ton haut /H/ s’oppose à une absence de ton (il n’y a pas de ton bas phonologique en shingazidja). Comme c’est le cas dans d’autres langues bantoues 6 (Philippson 1991), les tons hauts se déplacent dans cette langue vers la droite aussi loin qu’ils le peuvent, jusqu’à ce qu’ils soient bloqués par un autre ton ou, j’y reviendrai, par une frontière de groupe prosodique.
tone_statements.translation: The tone system of Shingazidja is well known; ... This language has a so-called 'privative' system (cf. Hyman 2001), in which a high tone /H/ contrasts with the absence of tone (there is no phonological low tone in Shingazidja). As in other Bantu languages [fn.6] (Philippson 1991), high tones move rightward in this language as far as they can, until they are blocked by another tone or, as I will come back to, by a prosodic-group boundary.
tone_statements.locator: p.98, section 2 'Le système tonal du shingazidja'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Privative system: /H/ vs zero, unbounded rightward H shift, OCP deletion; separate 'accent de groupe' on the phrase penult (fn.8: tone-accent interactions unstudied). Fn.7: H lower after H (marked !).

tone_statements.quote: The major characteristics of the Shingazidja tone system are discussed in Tucker & Bryan (1970), ... A H tone shifts rightward. It shifts right to the end of a phonological phrase (j), unless it is blocked by a syllable bearing an underlying tone. ... The shift of the tone leads to the deletion of every even-numbered tone (in accordance with the Obligatory Contour Principle). ... Tone is not bounded by the edges of the prosodic word
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Underlying H vs toneless syllables; H shifts right to phrase end, even-numbered H deleted; toneless words get penult surface H; successive phrasal Hs downstep (p.127). No count; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Patin, Cédric (2010). The prosody of Shingazidja relatives. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 53 (Papers from the Workshop on Bantu Relative Clauses): 187-210. DOI 10.21248/zaspil.53.2010.398. (HAL halshs-00725784, record only.)
tone_statements.quote: The major characteristics of the Shingazidja tone system are well known. ... In Shingazidja, a high tone shifts to its right up to the end of a Phonological Phrase,2 except if an underlying tone-bearing unit blocks it. The shift of the tone leads to the deletion of every even-numbered tone (in respect of the Obligatory Contour Principle). In (1bi) 3 for instance, the tone of the noun maβáha4 ‘cats’ shifts to the penult of the adjective mailí ‘two’, and the tone of the adjective is thus deleted.
tone_statements.summary: High tones (vs. toneless vowels) shift rightward to the phonological-phrase end; even-numbered tones delete (OCP); no tone count; utterance-final downstep only mentioned; stress mentioned in passing.

tone_statements.citation: Patin, Cédric (2008). Focus and phrasing in Shingazidja. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 49: 167-189. DOI 10.21248/zaspil.49.2008.369.
tone_statements.quote: Evidence for phrasing in Shingazidja comes from the shift of tone. In this language, a high tone will shift to the syllable preceding another tone bearing syllable (see section 2.1), the last syllable of a phonological phrase (see section 2.2) or the penultimate syllable of an intonational phrase (see section 2.3). ... Shingazidja ... exhibits an ‘unbounded’ tone shift phenomenon. In (2-a), the noun waleví ‘drunkards’ has a high tone on its final syllable in isolation. ... The noun, which underlyingly bears a high tone on its last syllable, is then fully low.
tone_statements.locator: p. 169, section 2 'Phrasing in Shingazidja' and section 2.1 'Tone phenomena'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Lexical high tones (vs toneless) on syllables, unbounded rightward shift, OCP deletion; no tone count; IP-final syllable extraprosodic, final tone lowered; nothing on word stress. At least 15 forms.

tone_statements.quote: Le comorien est une langue purement accentuelle. Au niveau lexical, les syllabes se divisent en marquées et non-marquées. Il n'y a normalement pas plus d'une syllabe marquée par morphème [...] [fn.1] Il convient cependant d'indiquer que, dans le dialecte ngazija, un petit nombre de nominaux dérivés du bantu commun ont deux syllabes marquées. A ma connaissance, ce n'est pas le cas en ndzuani. [...] 3.8.1. Une particularité du comorien est que les pieds ne se forment qu'au niveau post-lexical [...] - la syllabe finale est extra-métrique (sauf si elle est marquée) - construire des pieds illimités et dominants à gauche - chaque pied est affecté d'un H sur sa syllabe finale - les H sont tous effacés à l'exception du premier du groupe.
tone_statements.translation: Comorian is a purely accentual language. At the lexical level, syllables divide into marked and unmarked. There is normally no more than one marked syllable per morpheme [...] [fn.1] It should however be noted that in the Ngazija dialect a small number of nominals inherited from Common Bantu have two marked syllables. To my knowledge this is not the case in Ndzuani. [...] 3.8.1. A peculiarity of Comorian is that feet are only built post-lexically [...] - the final syllable is extrametrical (unless marked) - build unbounded left-dominant feet - each foot receives an H on its final syllable - all H are deleted except the first of the group.
tone_statements.locator: Chapitre cinq §3.8 'Le comorien (dialecte ndzuani)', pp.350-351 with fn.1-2; Ngazija diachrony Chapitre final §2.2.3 pp.421-423
tone_statements.summary: Privative lexical 'marked vs unmarked' syllables (reflex of Proto-Bantu H), realized post-lexically as H tones on the final syllable of unbounded left-dominant feet within the phonological phrase, final syllable extrametrical, only the first H of a group surviving (Ndzuani; Ngazija differs in allowing two marked syllables per stem and in pairing feet); i.e. a tonal/pitch accent system, no separat…

readall_conflicts: Neither listed work could be opened beyond its theses.fr abstract, so nothing new contradicts the catalog outright. The one tension is in Rey 1990's abstract, which divides words into 'oxyton ou paroxyton' (final- vs penult-accented) with accent placement predictable by phonological rule, whereas the catalog codes a single fixed: penultimate syllable rule; this is the same final-vs-penult split that Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1989 derive from the H-tone system (toneless words get penult prominence, H-final words are final-prominent), so it refines rather than overturns the penult default. Patin's open 2018 paper held by the project (not a listed work) states stress is aligned with the penult of the phrase, i.e. the stress domain is the phonological phrase, with tone separately able to surface on the final; Patin 2007's abstract is about tone only.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at Patin 2016 p.290 in the publisher PDF we hold; locator correct. (2) The classification (fixed penult, weight-blind, coexisting with a privative H tone system) rests on the language's leading prosody specialist, and his later open papers downloaded now (TAL 2018, SPiL Plus 2021) restate it: the penult (of the phrase) is the stressed syllable, lengthened, with tone/vowel-aperture interactions. Nothing found contradicts penult stress. Two refinements worth a caution line rather than a reclassify: (a) Patin 2018/2021 phrase the domain as 'penult of the phrase' (2016: penult of words, strengthened phrase-penult), so the word domain field is the 2016 wording and the phrase reading is at least as well supported; (b) the older French/Illinois tradition (Lafon 1988 pp.397-398. sources.quote: In this section we examine the tonology of Shingazidja, a Bantu language, closely related to Kiswahili, which is spoken on the largest of the Comoros Islands, Ngazidja. Unlike Kiswahili, which lost the Proto-Bantu tonal system and replaced it with penultimate stress, Shingazidja has retained a system of tonal contrasts, and a complex surface tonal pattern
sources.note: Explicitly contrasts Swahili's penultimate stress with Shingazidja's retained tonal contrasts; H domains align with the right edge of the Prosodic Phrase, final syllable excluded (Nonfinality), so surface H lands on the phrase penult. Silent on whether Shingazidja also has a stress/lengthening on the penult; treats 'accent' as tone.
sources.venue: ROA-176 (published in Hyman & Kisseberth eds., Theoretical aspects of Bantu tone, CSLI)

sources.quote: [p.396] Nous ne traiterons pas des phénomènes supra-segmentaux, qu'il s'agisse de l'accentuation ou de l'intonation lexicale: en effet, nos données ne sont pas suffisament fiables sur ce point. [p.397] Par contre, l'accentuation se manifeste, tant au niveau lexical qu'en énoncé. [...] En isolation, les mots de plus d'une syllabe se partagent en deux classes: les mots accentués sur la pénultième et ceux accentués sur la dernière syllabe. [...] a) polysyllabes accentués sur la pénultième. Ce schème d'accentuation est, de loin, le plus fréquent [...] Toutefois, il arrive aussi que l'accent se maintienne sur la même syllabe malgré un allongement du mot, notamment avec l'extension -ih- : [mbi'hanyo], désordre [p.398] [mbi'hanyiho], confusion |mu-bih-any-ih-o| [...] b) polyssyllabes [sic] accentués sur la dernière syllabe Quelques mots ne suivent pas ce comportement et sont accentués sur la dernière syllabe; la place de l'accent est parfois alors distinctive: ['raha], joie (ar.) ≠ [ra'ha], pas encore; ['hadja], besoin (ar.) ≠ [ha'dja], il/elle est venu; [tsi'hama], j'ai trait ≠ [ha'ma], comme (ar.). Parmi ces 'paires', au moins un des termes est d'origine arabe.
sources.locator: vol. II, 'Phénomènes supra-segmentaux: accent, tons' and 'Accentuation', printed pp.396-398 (HAL tel-00131147, =, PDF pp.167-169); 'Ton ou accent ?' pp.398-400
sources.note: First-hand (the author's 1976-78 fieldwork, isolated words, impressionistic; he warns on p.396 that his suprasegmental data are not reliable and gives only 'une observation très générale'). Penultimate accent is 'de loin le plus fréquent' on isolated polysyllables; a few words are accented on the final syllable, with distinctive pairs in which at least one member is an Arabic loan; the accent can stay on its syllable under the extension -ih- (antepenult in [mbi'hanyiho], [zi'fanyiha]); monosyllables bear the accent; no tone system was isolated; pp.398-400 report Philippson's metrical reading in which the 'accentogène' syllables correspond to Guthrie's High tones. Same default placement as the catalog (penult) plus a listed exception set = refines under the reading protocol (exceptions, weight, domain refine; a different placement or type contradicts); the penult/final split is the one Rey 1990 ('mot oxyton ou paroxyton') and Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1989 (H-toned finals not extrametrical) describe, both carried as refinements on this page.

sources.quote: Le système tonal du shingazidja est bien connu ; ... Cette langue présente un système dit ‘privatif’ (cf. Hyman 2001), dans lequel un ton haut /H/ s’oppose à une absence de ton (il n’y a pas de ton bas phonologique en shingazidja). Comme c’est le cas dans d’autres langues bantoues 6 (Philippson 1991), les tons hauts se déplacent dans cette langue vers la droite aussi loin qu’ils le peuvent, jusqu’à ce qu’ils soient bloqués par un autre ton ou, j’y reviendrai, par une frontière de groupe prosodique.

sources.quote: The major characteristics of the Shingazidja tone system are well known. ... In Shingazidja, a high tone shifts to its right up to the end of a Phonological Phrase,2 except if an underlying tone-bearing unit blocks it. The shift of the tone leads to the deletion of every even-numbered tone (in respect of the Obligatory Contour Principle). In (1bi) 3 for instance, the tone of the noun maβáha4 ‘cats’ shifts to the penult of the adjective mailí ‘two’, and the tone of the adjective is thus deleted.
sources.note: High tones (vs. toneless vowels) shift rightward to the phonological-phrase end; even-numbered tones delete (OCP); no tone count; utterance-final downstep only mentioned; stress mentioned in passing.

sources.citation: Patin, Cédric (2008). Focus and phrasing in Shingazidja. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 49: 167-189. DOI 10.21248/zaspil.49.2008.369.
sources.quote: Evidence for phrasing in Shingazidja comes from the shift of tone. In this language, a high tone will shift to the syllable preceding another tone bearing syllable (see section 2.1), the last syllable of a phonological phrase (see section 2.2) or the penultimate syllable of an intonational phrase (see section 2.3). ... Shingazidja ... exhibits an ‘unbounded’ tone shift phenomenon. In (2-a), the noun waleví ‘drunkards’ has a high tone on its final syllable in isolation. ... The noun, which underlyingly bears a high tone on its last syllable, is then fully low.
sources.locator: p. 169, section 2 'Phrasing in Shingazidja' and section 2.1 'Tone phenomena'
sources.note: Lexical high tones (vs toneless) on syllables, unbounded rightward shift, OCP deletion; no tone count; IP-final syllable extraprosodic, final tone lowered; nothing on word stress. At least 15 forms.

sources.quote: Le comorien est une langue purement accentuelle. Au niveau lexical, les syllabes se divisent en marquées et non-marquées. Il n'y a normalement pas plus d'une syllabe marquée par morphème [...] [fn.1] Il convient cependant d'indiquer que, dans le dialecte ngazija, un petit nombre de nominaux dérivés du bantu commun ont deux syllabes marquées. A ma connaissance, ce n'est pas le cas en ndzuani. [...] 3.8.1. Une particularité du comorien est que les pieds ne se forment qu'au niveau post-lexical [...] - la syllabe finale est extra-métrique (sauf si elle est marquée) - construire des pieds illimités et dominants à gauche - chaque pied est affecté d'un H sur sa syllabe finale - les H sont tous effacés à l'exception du premier du groupe.

tone.translation: Comorian is a purely accentual language. At the lexical level, syllables divide into marked and unmarked. There is normally no more than one marked syllable per morpheme [...] [fn.1] It should however be noted that in the Ngazija dialect a small number of nominals inherited from Common Bantu have two marked syllables. To my knowledge this is not the case in Ndzuani. [...] 3.8.1. A peculiarity of Comorian is that feet are only built post-lexically [...] - the final syllable is extrametrical (unless marked) - build unbounded left-dominant feet - each foot receives an H on its final syllable - all H are deleted except the first of the group.
tone.summary: Privative lexical 'marked vs unmarked' syllables (reflex of Proto-Bantu H), realized post-lexically as H tones on the final syllable of unbounded left-dominant feet within the phonological phrase, final syllable extrametrical, only the first H of a group surviving (Ndzuani; Ngazija differs in allowing two marked syllables per stem and in pairing feet); i.e. a tonal/pitch accent system, no separat…
